title: Introduction to Clinical Medicine: History and Examination
description: Clinical history taking, general and systemic examination, clinical reasoning, and communication skills for students starting clinical postings.

topics.title: Taking a Clinical History
topics.summary: Structure of the history, the presenting complaint, systems review, and communication.

notes.b: The clinical history is the most important diagnostic tool. Structure: biodata (name, age, sex, occupation, address, ethnicity, religion); presenting complaint(s) in the patient's words with duration; history of presenting complaint (onset, character, progression, associated symptoms, relieving/aggravating factors, relevant negatives); review of systems; past medical and surgical history (including previous admissions, transfusions, chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, sickle cell disease, TB, HIV); drug history (prescribed, over-the-counter, herbal and traditional medicines, allergies); family history; social history (alcohol, tobacco, occupation, living conditions, finances); and in women the gynaecological and obstetric history. Pain is characterised using SOCRATES: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity.
k: Presenting complaint in the patient's words
Ask about herbal and traditional medicines

notes.b: Good consultations begin with introduction, consent and ensuring privacy; use open questions first, then closed questions for detail; listen actively; avoid jargon; use interpreters (Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Pidgin and other languages) rather than relying on relatives for sensitive issues; explore the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE); summarise and check understanding. Respect cultural and religious beliefs. Confidentiality and informed consent are ethical requirements. Collateral history from relatives is important for children, unconscious or confused patients.

topics.title: General Examination
topics.summary: First impressions, vital signs and the head-to-toe general examination.

notes.b: Examination starts with general inspection: does the patient look well or ill, distressed, breathless, in pain; posture, gait, nutritional status (BMI, wasting), hydration and level of consciousness (AVPU or GCS). Vital signs: temperature, pulse (rate, rhythm, volume, character), blood pressure (both arms initially), respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. The general examination (often summarised as looking for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, oedema and dehydration) should use good daylight: pallor in conjunctivae, palms and nail beds (easier than skin in dark-skinned patients); jaundice in the sclerae and under the tongue; central cyanosis on the tongue and lips.
k: Pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, oedema
Check conjunctivae and palms for pallor

notes.b: Finger clubbing (loss of the nail-fold angle, increased curvature) occurs in chronic suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema), lung cancer, cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, liver cirrhosis and inflammatory bowel disease — not in uncomplicated asthma or COPD. Lymph nodes are examined for size, consistency, tenderness, matting and fixation (e.g. matted nodes in TB; hard fixed nodes in malignancy). Pitting oedema is graded by extent (ankle, knee, sacrum in bedridden patients). Dehydration signs include dry mucosa, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes and fontanelle (infants) and tachycardia.

topics.title: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Examination
topics.summary: Pulse, JVP, apex beat, heart sounds and murmurs; chest inspection, percussion and auscultation.

notes.b: Sequence: inspection, palpation, percussion (rarely) and auscultation. The radial pulse is assessed for rate and rhythm; the carotid for character (slow-rising in aortic stenosis; collapsing/water-hammer in aortic regurgitation). Jugular venous pressure (JVP) is measured with the patient at 45° as the vertical height above the sternal angle (normal ≤ 3–4 cm) — raised in right heart failure, fluid overload and pericardial disease. The apex beat is normally at the 5th left intercostal space in the midclavicular line; displaced laterally in left ventricular dilatation. Auscultate the mitral (apex), tricuspid (left lower sternal edge), pulmonary (left 2nd ICS) and aortic (right 2nd ICS) areas. Systolic murmurs: aortic stenosis (ejection systolic, radiates to the carotids), mitral regurgitation (pansystolic, radiates to the axilla); diastolic murmurs: mitral stenosis (mid-diastolic rumble at the apex — rheumatic heart disease), aortic regurgitation (early diastolic at the left sternal edge). Rheumatic heart disease remains important in Nigeria.
k: JVP at 45°, normal ≤ 3–4 cm above sternal angle

notes.b: Inspect for respiratory rate, use of accessory muscles, chest shape (barrel chest in COPD, pectus deformities), symmetry of expansion and scars. Palpate the trachea (deviated away from tension pneumothorax and large effusion, towards collapse and fibrosis), chest expansion and tactile fremitus. Percussion: resonant (normal), dull (consolidation, collapse), stony dull (pleural effusion), hyper-resonant (pneumothorax, emphysema). Auscultation: vesicular breath sounds (normal), bronchial breathing (consolidation), reduced sounds (effusion, pneumothorax), crackles (fluid — pulmonary oedema, pneumonia, fibrosis), wheeze (airway narrowing — asthma, COPD) and pleural rub. Vocal resonance is increased in consolidation and decreased in effusion.

topics.title: Abdominal and Neurological Examination
topics.summary: Inspection, palpation for organomegaly, ascites; cranial nerves, motor and sensory examination.

notes.b: With the patient supine and relaxed, inspect (distension — fat, fluid, flatus, faeces, fetus; scars; visible peristalsis; distended veins; stigmata of liver disease such as spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia). Palpate lightly then deeply in all regions, watching the patient's face for tenderness, guarding and rebound (peritonism). Palpate the liver (from the right iliac fossa upwards with respiration) and spleen (from the right iliac fossa towards the left costal margin — splenomegaly is common in Nigeria from malaria, sickle cell disease in young children, schistosomiasis, leukaemias and lymphomas); ballot the kidneys. Detect ascites by shifting dullness and fluid thrill. Auscultate bowel sounds (absent in ileus/peritonitis; high-pitched tinkling in obstruction). Examine the hernial orifices and external genitalia, and perform a digital rectal examination when indicated (with a chaperone).
k: Palpate from the RIF for liver and spleen

notes.b: Neurological examination covers higher mental function (GCS, orientation, speech), cranial nerves (I–XII), motor system (inspection for wasting and fasciculation, tone, power graded 0–5, reflexes, coordination), sensory system (light touch, pain, temperature, vibration, proprioception in dermatomal or peripheral nerve patterns) and gait. Upper motor neuron lesions: increased tone (spasticity), weakness in a pyramidal pattern, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar (Babinski) response, clonus. Lower motor neuron lesions: wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes, flexor plantars. Meningism: neck stiffness, Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign.

topics.title: Clinical Reasoning, Case Presentation and Documentation
topics.summary: Building differential diagnoses, choosing investigations, presenting cases and writing notes.

notes.b: Clinical reasoning integrates history, examination and investigations to reach a diagnosis. Approaches include pattern recognition (fast, experience-based) and hypothetico-deductive reasoning (generating a list of hypotheses and testing them). A differential diagnosis lists possible causes ranked by likelihood and seriousness — never miss treatable or dangerous conditions ('can't-miss diagnoses'). Consider common local conditions first (in Nigeria: malaria, typhoid, TB, HIV, sickle cell disease, hypertension, diabetes), while remembering that 'common things are common' but co-infection is frequent. Cognitive biases include anchoring (fixing on an early diagnosis), premature closure and availability bias. Investigations should be chosen to answer specific questions, considering cost and availability.
k: Rank differentials by likelihood and danger

notes.b: A case presentation is concise and structured: biodata and presenting complaint, key positive and negative findings from the history and examination, a summary (e.g. 'a 25-year-old man with 2 weeks of fever, weight loss and cough with haemoptysis'), a differential diagnosis with reasoning, and a management plan (investigations, treatment, monitoring, counselling). Clinical notes must be legible, dated, timed and signed with the author's name and designation, using approved abbreviations; the SOAP format (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) is widely used for progress notes. Records are legal documents and must be kept confidential.
